passage: I'm Himani, Sarita's roommate at the B.Ed hostel. On Friday we got our teaching-practice feedback forms from the schools we'd been placed in. Sarita's form was mostly fours and fives out of five. The comments said things like 'children respond warmly' and 'well-planned lessons'. One box, classroom control, had a 2 and a frowning face drawn next to it by the supervising teacher. That evening Sarita lay on her bed with the form on her chest. 'I'm a terrible teacher,' she said. 'Did you see the face?' I read out the fives. She said, 'Anyone can plan lessons.' She put the form in a drawer without reading it again. I can't know what she's feeling inside. But from where I sit, one frowning face seems to weigh more than the whole page.

qa.a: Sarita got a 2 for classroom control.

qa.q: Why does Sarita say 'Anyone can plan lessons'?
qa.a: The frowning face hurts so much that it feels like the true verdict, so Sarita dismisses the good comments to keep the picture of herself as a terrible teacher.

qa.q: What could Sarita do with the form instead of putting it in a drawer?
qa.a: Sarita could reread every box, note the fours and fives beside the 2, and then ask the supervising teacher for one tip on classroom control.

qa.q: How does Himani see the form compared with how Sarita sees it?
qa.a: Himani sees a strong form with one area to work on, and seems worried that the focus on one face is turning Sarita's success into a failure.

Tuesday: After her marketing presentation, Ishita collected twenty-six peer feedback slips. Twenty-four were kind: 'confident', 'great visuals', 'best one today'. One said 'too fast'. One had a frowning face and the word 'boring'. On the metro home she read the 'boring' one nine times.
Thursday: Pranav, her project partner, asked how it went. 'Badly,' she said. 'People found it boring.' 'People?' 'Well. Someone.'
Saturday: Pranav spread all twenty-six slips on the library table and had her sort them into two piles. The good pile covered half the table. The other pile was two slips. Ishita looked at it for a while. 'I'll slow down next time,' she said. 'The boring one I'll just leave.'

qa.q: How many peer feedback slips did Ishita collect?
qa.a: Ishita collected twenty-six peer feedback slips.

qa.q: Why did 'People found it boring' feel true to Ishita on Thursday?
qa.a: Reading the 'boring' slip nine times made it loud in Ishita's mind, so one person's comment felt like everyone's view and the success felt like a failure.

qa.q: What turning point came on Saturday, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Sorting all twenty-six slips into two piles showed twenty-four good ones against two, and Ishita took one useful fix, slowing down, while letting the 'boring' slip go.

qa.q: What might Pranav have noticed when Ishita said 'Well. Someone'?
qa.a: Pranav may have realised the problem wasn't the presentation but how the feedback was being read, which is why Pranav chose to lay out every slip.

grounding: Shows a student who fixes on one frowning 'boring' slip among twenty-six mostly good ones, until all the feedback is laid out.

passage: Dhruv, you've been scowling at that internship review since dinner. Here's something from my own college days, when I was twenty. I remember one line, word for word, forty years later: 'Needs to ask more questions.' I remember nothing else. Your Chachi found that page last year in an old file and read it to me. It said I was reliable, quick to learn, good with the drawing team, and that they would hire me again. I carried one line for forty years and dropped the rest the day I got it. It made me feel like a failure when I had actually done well. So, Manoj Chacha is asking: read me yours. The whole page.

qa.a: Manoj asks Dhruv to read the whole page aloud, so every good comment is heard next to the one that hurts before Dhruv decides what the review means.

grounding: Shows an uncle recalling how one critical line from an internship review stayed with him for forty years while all the praise was forgotten.

passage:
The last bus from the hotel to the college hostel was packed, and Shankar stood squeezed near the door with his phone at five percent. He opened the internship feedback form that Lokesh, the kitchen supervisor, had just emailed.

Hygiene: 5/5. Teamwork: 5/5, "always helps others." Punctuality: 5/5. Knife skills: 4/5, "improving fast." Attitude: 5/5, "a pleasure to have." Plating speed: 2/5, with a frowning face: "Too slow during rush hour."

The bus lurched. The phone died.

All the way back, Shankar saw only that frowning face. Too slow. He imagined Lokesh telling the other chefs. He imagined the hotel never hiring him.

In the hostel, his roommate asked how the feedback was.

"Bad," Shankar said. "I'm too slow. I don't think I'm cut out for kitchens."

He went to bed without charging the phone, as if the rest of the form might not exist if he didn't look.

qa.q: What score did Shankar get for plating speed?
Why did the frowning face stay with Shankar all the way back?
qa.a: It was the only line that stung, and with the phone dead, his mind replayed it until it grew into never being hired. The five-out-of-fives faded because they didn't hurt.

qa.q: What could Shankar do the next morning to see the form more clearly?
qa.a: Charge the phone, read every score, and write the good ones next to the one to improve. Then he could ask Lokesh for tips on plating faster.

qa.q: How might Lokesh see Shankar's internship, judging from the form?
qa.a: Lokesh seems to see a helpful, punctual intern who is a pleasure to have and just needs to get faster at plating. The frowning face was one note, not a verdict.

grounding: A student fixes on one frowning comment on an internship feedback form and forgets the many good ones, so success feels like failure.

subtype: Only the negatives in a review [Actor]
passage:
On the terrace of their college in Jadavpur, Arnab sat with a stack of feedback slips from the Saturday science workshop he'd run for Class 6 kids.

Kalyani flipped through them. "Arnab, these are lovely. 'Best Saturday ever.' 'I understood magnets for the first time.' 'Please come again.' There are thirty of these!"

"Read the one on top."

She did. In wobbly pencil: "It was a bit boring when he talked too long."

"That one," Arnab said. "That's the true one. The others are just being nice."

"Thirty kids being nice?"

"Kids are honest when they're bored. That's the one that counts."

Kalyani put the slip at the bottom of the pile. He took it out and put it back on top.

"I don't think I'll do the next workshop," he said. "It clearly didn't work."

qa.q: How many feedback slips were lovely, according to Kalyani?
Why does Arnab believe the one negative slip is "the true one"?
qa.a: The criticism stings, so his mind treats it as more honest than the praise. Filtering this way makes a successful workshop feel like a failure.

qa.q: What went wrong in how Arnab read the slips, and what could fix it?
qa.a: He let one comment outweigh thirty, and was ready to quit because of it. He could count both piles and use the one note as a tip to talk less and do more activities.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel when Arnab puts the slip back on top?
qa.a: Kalyani might feel frustrated and a bit sad, since she can see how well the workshop went. She seems to want him to notice what the children loved.

grounding: A student reads thirty warm feedback slips and one critical one, fixes on the single negative, and feels the successful workshop failed.
